cues.text: Let us now turn to the sixth chapter, where we apply the MIND CA approach to strategy and to phased innovation.
The title already carries two ideas.
One is strategy, meaning the deliberate choices an organisation makes about where and how to create value.
The other is phased innovation, meaning that change is introduced in stages rather than all at once.
Begin with the MTN case.
In this case, MoMo, MTN's mobile money service, is positioned as a strategic service.
That wording matters.
MoMo is not treated as a side product or a technical add-on.
It is a service that responds to two pressures: competition from other providers, and the changing needs of customers.
When a service is strategic, decisions about its technology must follow from those business pressures, not the other way round.
Now consider a tempting shortcut.
Someone might say: let us simply take the old application and move it onto new infrastructure.
This is called rehosting.
The source is clear that rehosting the old application alone would not fix two deeper problems.
The first is siloed ownership, where different teams each own a fragment of the system and nobody owns the whole customer outcome.
The second is release queues, where changes wait in line for approval or deployment slots.
Notice that both problems are organisational.
They sit in how people and teams work, so moving the same code to a new server leaves them untouched.
This is a good reminder of the difference between digitalisation and genuine digital transformation.
Changing the technology platform is not enough if the operating model stays the same.
So what does the case propose instead?
Two things.
First, a platform team.
Second, a standard delivery pipeline.
A platform team builds and maintains shared foundations that other teams can use.
A delivery pipeline is the standard, automated route by which code moves from development through testing to release.
Together, they create reusable capabilities.
Instead of every team solving the same problems again, teams draw on common tools and routes.
That reduces queues and weakens the silos.
Next, the Strangler Fig pattern.
Picture a strangler fig tree growing around a host tree.
Gradually, the new growth takes over.
In software, the Strangler Fig pattern works in the same way.
Selected functionality is gradually routed to new services, while the old system continues serving all the other operations.
At no point do you switch everything off and hope the replacement works.
The old and the new live side by side, and traffic moves piece by piece.
That is what makes the approach safer for a service people depend on.
Now to the second block, which explains how to stage the investment.
A staged investment can begin with a comparatively low-criticality service, and the example is a notification service.
Why start there?
Because if something goes wrong with a notification, the harm is smaller than if money is lost.
In this first stage, the team does three things.
It measures reliability.
It prevents duplicate SMS, so a customer does not receive the same message twice.
And it expands to higher-risk domains only when the controls work.
That last condition is crucial.
Expansion is earned by evidence, not by calendar.
Contrast this with critical money movement.
When money moves, four things are required.
First, durable idempotency.
Idempotency means that performing the same request more than once has the same effect as performing it once.
So if a network failure causes a payment request to be sent twice, the customer is not charged twice.
Durable means this protection survives failures and restarts.
Second, accurate ledger invariants.
A ledger is the record of accounts and transactions, and an invariant is a rule that must always remain true, for example that the books balance.
Third, reconciliation, which is the checking of records against one another to confirm they agree.
Fourth, tested recovery, meaning the ability to restore a correct state after failure has actually been tried and proven, not merely assumed.
The source calls this an example of stage-gated transformation combined with iterative delivery.
Stage-gated means progress passes through gates, and you move forward only when criteria are met.
Iterative delivery means releasing in repeated cycles, learning and improving each time.
Put together, you move in steps, and each step must pass a check.
The block then introduces the canary.
A 5% canary exposes a small, controlled share of eligible traffic to a new version before expansion.
The name comes from the old practice of using canary birds as early warning in mines.
Here, five percent of eligible traffic acts as the early warning.
If the new version misbehaves, only a small portion of users is affected.
Note the word eligible: not all traffic qualifies.
And then comes an important qualification.
It is not appropriate to assume that every operation can be retried or rolled back harmlessly.
Sending a notification again may be an annoyance.
Repeating or undoing a money transfer can be serious, because the effects may already have reached other systems or other people.
So the safety of retry and rollback has to be checked operation by operation.
Finally, the third block gives the roadmap.
It has six phases, in this order: discovery, pilot, controlled migration, evaluation, scale, and legacy retirement.
Discovery is where you understand the situation.
Pilot is a small trial.
Controlled migration moves selected parts carefully.
Evaluation assesses the results.
Scale extends what has worked.
Legacy retirement switches off the old system once it is no longer needed.
The source adds that you should define decision gates with measurable thresholds.
A gate needs a number or a clear test, so the decision to proceed is based on evidence, such as reliability measures, and not on opinion.
The closing principle ties everything together.
A microservice architecture is a means to business agility, not a goal detached from value.
Microservices are one way of building a system as small, independent services.
They are worth adopting only to the extent that they help the business respond faster and serve customers better.
If they do not, they are simply complexity.
The goal is business value, and the architecture is the tool.
